editor_spans.body: The Motherwell speech does more than offer a devolution deal. It tries to change what Scottish politics argues about. Since 2014 the dividing line has been nation against nation. Burnham sets Ravenscraig beside the Leigh coalfield and insists the problems on both sides of the border are 'more similar' than different. That replaces the constitutional question with a place-versus-centre one. It is a unionist argument that never says the word union.

The detail also complicates the suspicion that the offer is a way to go around Holyrood. The most concrete item, devolving DWP employment support, would hand a reserved Westminster function to Scotland, 'shaped by Holyrood'. Burnham is pressing Edinburgh to push power down while giving it more to push.

The scale is the weakness. By his own account the Ravenscraig site is still being filled more than thirty years after closure. Against that, the speech offers two defence colleges funded with £10 million from each government, a share of £1 billion of research money spread across the whole UK, and devolved say over innovation and employability budgets. Letting regions decide how to spend modest sums is not the same as rebuilding an industrial base. The pieces most likely to move that needle, such as shipbuilding, Grangemouth and energy jobs, stay with the central governments.

The most radical line was about procurement. Burnham boasts of paying more so Greater Manchester's buses were built in Falkirk, and wants all UK public buying to work that way. That cuts against decades of Treasury value-for-money rules that pick the cheapest bid. It would also run into the UK's international procurement commitments. Asked why reindustrialisation has not happened, he answers with this, not devolution. It is also the one lever that can only be pulled from the centre.

The first test is the National Economic Council meeting with the devolved first ministers, the first since he took office. If an SNP government accepts an offer framed as 'place first, not party first', Burnham will have changed the terms of the union argument. If it refuses, his reframing will have been a campaign message for Scottish Labour.
